Consider the set $A,$ shown above. The boundary of $A$ is given by

$$
∂A=\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,\bbox[5px,border:1px solid black]{\phantom{AAAAA}}\,\}.
$$

What is the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
The boundary of a set $A,$ denoted $∂A,$ is the set that contains all the boundary points of $A.$

The set $A$ and its boundary $∂A$ are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14162460/assets/d7293d96b71f573dbdcbfb491646f0e563f8ad1567eab5baaf960533e72d473f.png)

From the diagram, the boundary points of $A$ lie on the line $y=2-x.$

Therefore, 

$$
∂A=\{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,y=2-x\,\}.
$$

questions.problem:
Compute $P(X\ge 3)$ given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-\frac{1}{3}x},\, & x\ge 0, \\ 0,\, & x<0.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
If a continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function $f(x),$ then 

$$
P(a<X<b)={\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

So, in our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 3) & =P(3\le X<\infty ) \\  & ={\int }_{3}^{\infty }f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{3}^{\infty }\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-\frac{1}{3}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[-{e}^{-\frac{1}{3}x}]}_{3}^{\infty } \\  & ={e}^{-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given the two planes $3x-y+z=0$ and $x-z+4=0$, which of the following statements are true?

I. The cross product of the normal vectors of the planes is equal to $0.$

II. The planes are parallel.

III. The planes intersect on a line.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that:

- For the plane $3x-y+z=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨3,-1,1⟩.$

- For the plane $x-z+4=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,0,-1⟩.$

Now, let's consider the statements.

- Statement I is false. Computing the cross product of the normal vectors, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨3,-1,1⟩\times ⟨1,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 3 & -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =i+4j+k \\  & =⟨1,4,1⟩\ne 0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Since ${n}_{1}\times {n}_{2}\ne 0$, the vectors ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are not parallel. As a result, the planes are not parallel either.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, two non-parallel planes in $3$-dimensional space must intersect on a line.

Therefore, only statement III is true.

questions.problem:
| $f$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=4$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $X=1$ | $\frac{3}{20}$ | $\frac{7}{20}$ |
| $X=3$ | $\frac{9}{20}$ | $\frac{1}{20}$ |

Compute ${f}_{Y|X}(2\,|\,3)$ given that the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ shown in the table above.
questions.worked_solution:
The conditional probability mass function ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)$ is defined as

$$
{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=P(Y=y\,|\,X=x).
$$

Therefore, we're required to compute the conditional probability

$$
{f}_{Y|X}(2\,|\,3)=P(Y=2\,|\,X=3).
$$

By the multiplication law for conditional probability, we have

$$
P(Y=2\,|\,X=3)=\frac{P(X=3,Y=2)}{P(X=3)}=\frac{f(3,2)}{{f}_{X}(3)}
$$

where $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability mass function of $X$ and $Y,$ and ${f}_{X}(x)$ is the marginal distribution of $X.$

Recall that the marginal distribution for $X$ corresponds to the row totals. Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(3) & =f(3,2)+f(3,4) \\  & =\frac{9}{20}+\frac{1}{20} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given table, $f(3,2)=\frac{9}{20}.$ 

Finally, substituting  ${f}_{X}(3)=\frac{1}{2}$ and $f(3,2)=\frac{9}{20}$ in our formula above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y|X}(2\,|\,3) & =P(Y=2\,|\,X=3) \\  & =\frac{f(3,2)}{{f}_{X}(3)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{9}{20})}{(\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =\frac{9}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the set of matrices $\{A,B,C\},$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -1 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}4 & -4 \\ -8 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

 
If the set is linearly dependent, find the value of $\frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{2}}$ from a non-zero solution of ${x}_{1}A+{x}_{2}B+{x}_{3}C=O,$ where $O$ is the $2\times 2$ zero-matrix.
questions.worked_solution:
If the set is linearly dependent, then there exist ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}$ not all zero such that 

$$
{x}_{1}A+{x}_{2}B+{x}_{3}C=O.
$$

Otherwise, if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0,$ the set is linearly independent.

Substituting the matrices $A,$ $B,$ and $C$ into the above equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-3 & -1 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}4 & -4 \\ -8 & 0\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{1} \\ 0 & -2{x}_{1}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-3{x}_{2} & -{x}_{2} \\ 2{x}_{2} & 4{x}_{2}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4{x}_{3} & -4{x}_{3} \\ -8{x}_{3} & 0\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}+4{x}_{3} & {x}_{1}-{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3} \\ 2{x}_{2}-8{x}_{3} & -2{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding entries, we obtain the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}+4{x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{1}-{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3}=0 \\ 2{x}_{2}-8{x}_{3}=0 \\ -2{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we consider the corresponding augmented matrix and reduce it to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 4 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -8 & 0 \\ -2 & 4 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 8 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2} \\ {R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd.
Hence, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable.

The system is now

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}+4{x}_{3}=0 \\ 2{x}_{2}-8{x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

From the $2$nd equation, we get ${x}_{2}=4{x}_{3}.$ Substitute it into the first equation to get

$$
{x}_{1}-3(4{x}_{3})+4{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=8{x}_{3}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}8{x}_{3} \\ 4{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Finally, for any ${x}_{3}\ne 0,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{2}}=\frac{8{x}_{3}}{4{x}_{3}}=2.
$$

questions.problem:
The matrix $C$ and the vector $b$ are given below. Determine if $b\in \text{Col}(C).$ In the affirmative case, find the value of ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}$, where ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ are real numbers such that $b={x}_{1}{c}_{1}+{x}_{2}{c}_{2},$ and ${c}_{1},$ ${c}_{2}$ are the respective columns of $C.$

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 3 & -3\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}9 \\ -15\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
In order to determine whether $b$ lies in $\text{Col}(C),$ we need to check if the equation $Cx=b$ is consistent. So, let's find the row echelon form of the augmented matrix $[C\,|\,b]$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[C\,|\,b] & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 9 \\ 3 & -3 & -15\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 9 \\ 0 & 0 & 12\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=9 \\ 0=12.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get the false statement $0=12.$  

Therefore, the system is inconsistent, which implies that $b\notin \text{Col}(C).$

questions.problem:
The inverse of the matrix $Y$ is found using row operations, as shown below. What are the row operations corresponding to each step?

$$
\begin{aligned}[Y\,|\,I] & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \text{___________} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \text{___________} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We write down $Y$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply the standard Gauss-Jordan method to transform the matrix $Y$ into the identity matrix. We perform the same row operations on both matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}[Y\,|\,I\,] & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ -3 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding row operations are

$$
{R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+{R}_{2},\,{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1}.
$$

The matrix ${Y}^{-1}$ is given by the right-hand side of our big matrix after all of the transformations have been completed. Therefore, 

$$
{Y}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}].
$$
